abstract: Visual scenes anchor our experience of the world, yet the places in which scenes unfold are defined not only by what we see but also by what we smell. Whether and how odors contribute to the neural representation of visual scenes remains poorly understood. Here we asked whether a semantically congruent odor facilitates scene perception and identified the neural mechanisms supporting this facilitation. In two behavioral experiments, participants judged whether briefly presented, masked images depicted intact or scrambled scenes while continuously smelling an odor. A congruent odor lowered the exposure duration needed for accurate scene detection, and a placebo experiment, in which participants merely believed they were smelling an odor, failed to reproduce this benefit, indicating that the facilitation depends on actual sensory input rather than semantic priming. In an fMRI experiment, congruent odors enhanced responses and sharpened category-level scene representations in the parahippocampal place area (PPA), with the congruency-driven enhancement localized to the same anterior subregion that encoded scene identity. A conjunction analysis revealed superadditive responses to congruent odor-scene pairs in the orbitofrontal cortex (OFC) and hippocampus, and psychophysiological interaction analyses showed that congruent stimulation strengthened functional coupling among the OFC, PPA, and piriform cortex. Notably, the piriform cortex decoded visual scene identity after congruent odor-scene pairing, suggesting that odor-scene binding extends scene representations into primary olfactory cortex. Together, these findings identify the PPA as a site where olfactory signals refine the neural code for visual scenes and reveal an OFC-coordinated piriform-OFC-PPA network through which smell shapes our sense of place.
